dialogue.scene: Reem and her brother Faisal react to a news report saying teenagers spend seven hours a day on screens.

p1.t: Seven hours a day! That's shocking. I'd argue that phones have become far too addictive for people our age.
Come on, Reem. Not all screen time is a waste of time. I use my phone for homework too.
Sure, but how much of those seven hours is actually homework?
Fair question. Maybe an hour. The rest is probably games and videos, if I'm honest.

p2.t: Exactly. That's why I want to take a stand on this at home.

p1.t: I'd like to make a case for esports. Those players train eight hours a day, just like athletes.

dialogue.scene: Hind and Isabel must choose one charity project for their class during Ramadan.

p1.t: How about preparing iftar meals for workers? That would be really helpful.
It's a lovely idea. The problem with it is that it needs a lot of money and organising.
True. What about collecting clothes for families in need? That's worth considering.
Yes, it's easy, and everyone has clothes they don't wear.

p2.t: But would it make a real difference?
It depends on how many we collect. If every student brings five items, that's hundreds.
And the iftar meals?
We could do both. Clothes this week, and meals at the end of Ramadan with help from the parents.

I love it. It would keep the children entertained for ages. What do you reckon about face painting?
It's worth considering, but some little ones might be scared of the paint.
Fair enough. Shall we move on to the food, then?

p2.t: Sure. What do you think about a popcorn machine? Kids love watching it.
I'd go along with that, as long as an adult controls it.
Of course. Do you agree we should also give every child an Eidiya gift bag?

dialogue.scene: Mohammed and Abdullah are discussing how to spend the budget for improving the park in their neighbourhood. They must choose one main project.

p1.t: I think a big skate park would be the best choice. Teenagers have nowhere to go.
I see what you mean, but the park is mostly used by families with small children.
True. The problem with a playground, though, is that we already have one.
It's very old. And what about more trees? It's so hot in summer.

p2.t: I'm with you on the trees. Nobody can use the park at midday.
So why don't we meet halfway? Trees around a new playground, with a small skate area next to it.
That works for me. So shall we go for the playground and the trees as the main project?
Agreed. Let's settle on that, and suggest the skate area for next year.

dialogue.focus: So shall we go for the playground and the trees as the main project?

dialogue.scene: In a practice speaking exam, the examiner asks Abeer and Dana: Should schools teach life skills like cooking and managing money?

p1.t: That's an interesting question. Generally speaking, I'd say yes. Many teenagers can't even boil an egg!
Ha, that's true. In my experience, though, my parents taught me most life skills at home.
I see what you mean, but not every family has the time for that.
Fair point. And money is a good example. Lots of adults struggle with it. What's your view on that?

p2.t: I think managing money is the most important skill of all, especially with online shopping.
I'd agree. If students learnt to plan a budget, they'd make better choices later.
So maybe schools should teach money, and families can teach cooking?
That sounds like a sensible balance.

dialogue.focus: Generally speaking, I'd say yes.
qs: Who taught Dana most of her life skills?

dialogue.scene: In a mock speaking test, Salman and Jack discuss: How could young people be encouraged to read more? They must choose the two best ideas.

p1.t: Let's start with the reading competition. That would be motivating, especially with prizes.
Maybe, but the problem with competitions is that weaker readers might give up. What do you reckon about a book club?
I like it. Talking about books with friends makes reading more social.
And how about having audiobooks in the library? They're great for people who travel a lot.

p2.t: Good idea. We need to reach a decision, though. So shall we go for the book club and audiobooks?
I'd go along with that. They suit different types of readers.
Generally speaking, I think teenagers read more than adults think, just on screens.
I see what you mean, but reading a whole book is different from reading posts.

dialogue.focus: So shall we go for the book club and audiobooks?

qs: Do you prefer paper books, e-books or audiobooks? Why?
Should reading for pleasure be part of the school timetable?

words.ex: It's time our family took a stand on screen time.
I'd argue that phones help us learn more than they distract us.
My screen time doubles during the summer holidays.
Short-video apps are designed to be addictive.
Scrolling for hours is a complete waste of time.
My parents set limits on gaming during exam week.

dialogue.t: Seven hours a day! That's shocking. I'd argue that phones have become far too addictive for people our age.
Come on, Reem. Not all screen time is a waste of time. I use my phone for homework too.
Sure, but how much of those seven hours is actually homework?
Fair question. Maybe an hour. The rest is probably games and videos, if I'm honest.
Exactly. That's why I want to take a stand on this at home.
What do you mean? Are you going to ban phones at dinner?
Not ban them. I just think families should set limits on screen time, especially late at night.
That may be true, but teenagers also need to learn to control it themselves.

grammar.title: Stating a position
grammar.ar: ابدأ بـ I'd argue that لتعرض رأيك بثقة، ثم أضف سبباً واضحاً.
examples: I'd argue that phones should be switched off during lessons.
My position is simple: screen time needs limits.
The main reason I feel this way is that sleep matters.

words.ex: I'm convinced that a little homework helps us remember lessons.
That may be true, but students also need time to rest.
The whole point of practice is to get better.
If I miss a day, my assignments pile up quickly.
That's a fair point, but I still disagree.
I'd argue that weekends should be homework-free.

dialogue.t: I'm convinced that homework should be banned. By Thursday, everything starts to pile up and I can't relax.
I understand, but the whole point of homework is to practise what we learn in class.
That may be true, but we already practise for six hours a day at school.
That's a fair point. Still, some things, like vocabulary, need daily review.
So what are you suggesting? Homework every single night?
No, just short tasks. I'd argue that twenty minutes a day is enough.
Even so, some teachers give two hours. That's what I'm really against.
Then maybe we actually agree more than we thought.

grammar.title: Accepting a point, then disagreeing
grammar.ar: استخدم That may be true, but أو Even so لتقبل جزءاً من رأي الآخر ثم تدافع عن رأيك.
examples: That may be true, but it isn't the whole story.
You've made a fair point. Even so, I still think it's too much.
Although homework can help, two hours a night is unreasonable.

words.ex: Faisal made a strong case for esports at the Olympics.
By definition, a sport involves physical skill.
I know it's unpopular, but I stand by my opinion.
Swimming requires far more physical effort than gaming.
Pro gamers train their reaction time every day.
The coach took a stand on fair play.

dialogue.t: I'd like to make a case for esports. Those players train eight hours a day, just like athletes.
Training hard doesn't make it a sport. By definition, a sport needs physical effort.
But gaming at that level needs incredible reaction time and teamwork.
So does chess, and most people don't call chess a sport either.
Actually, the Olympic Committee does recognise chess as a sport.
Really? I didn't know that. Even so, sitting in a chair all day isn't athletic.
You can say that, but I stand by what I said. Skill and competition are what matter.
Well, let's agree to disagree. But you're coming to my tennis match on Friday.

grammar.title: Supporting your case
grammar.ar: قدّم موقفك بـ I'd like to make a case for، ثم ادعمه بتعريف أو مثال، وتمسّك به بـ I stand by.
examples: I'd like to make a case for esports as a school activity.
By definition, a sport involves competition and skill.
Even though some people disagree, I stand by my view.

words.ex: There's no doubt that sugary drinks are bad for our teeth.
In the long run, healthy habits save money.
You have a point, but students will just buy snacks outside.
Banning everything takes away freedom of choice.
Who is responsible for students' health at school?
The canteen could set limits on fizzy drinks.

dialogue.t: There's no doubt that the canteen sells too many crisps and fizzy drinks. I support the ban completely.
I'm not so sure. We're teenagers. Shouldn't we have some freedom of choice?
You have a point, but schools are responsible for keeping students healthy during the day.
Even so, if they ban everything, students will just bring snacks from home.
Maybe at first. But in the long run, people get used to healthier options.
So you'd remove chocolate completely? That sounds extreme.
Not completely. The canteen could set limits on sugary things, like one day a week.
Now that's a plan I could actually support.

grammar.title: Showing certainty and conceding
grammar.ar: عبّر عن يقينك بـ There's no doubt that، واعترف برأي الآخر بـ You have a point, but.
examples: There's no doubt that sugar affects concentration.
You have a point, but a total ban isn't realistic.
While students want choice, schools must think about health.

words.ex: I'm firmly in favour of keeping some lessons online.
Face-to-face lessons make it easier to ask questions.
Online courses let you study at your own pace.
Some students lose motivation when they study alone.
Online lessons are convenient. Even so, I miss my friends.
I'm convinced that teachers can't be replaced by apps.

dialogue.t: I'm firmly in favour of an online day. I could study at my own pace and sleep a bit longer.
Sleeping longer isn't really an argument, Dana!
Fine. But I'd argue that we'd also save time travelling and focus better at home.
Maybe you would. I'm convinced that most students would lose motivation without a teacher in the room.
That may be true for some students, but we already use the Madrasati platform easily.
Even so, face-to-face lessons are better for group work and asking quick questions.
While I agree group work is easier at school, one day a week wouldn't change that.
Okay, I'll tick 'not sure' instead of 'no'. You've half convinced me.

grammar.title: Concession with while / even so
grammar.ar: استخدم While في بداية الجملة لتعترف بنقطة، أو Even so بعد جملة لتعود إلى رأيك.
examples: While online lessons are flexible, they can feel lonely.
Classrooms can be noisy. Even so, I learn better there.
I'm firmly in favour of mixing both types of learning.

words.ex: The motion is that every teenager should volunteer.
Can you back up that claim with an example?
She answered every counter-argument calmly.
A good example can win the audience over.
He made a clear case for longer breaks.
That may be true, but it doesn't solve the problem.

dialogue.t: The motion is that teenagers should volunteer in the summer. I'd like to make a case for it.
Volunteering builds skills and confidence. My brother helped at Riyadh Season and now he's far more confident.
Thank you. One counter-argument is that teenagers need rest after a long school year.
Summer is our only chance to relax, travel with family and enjoy hobbies.
That may be true, but volunteering can be just a few hours a week.
Even so, forcing it would make it feel like more school. I'd argue it should be a choice.
I never said 'force'. I'd back up my point with the national target of one million volunteers.
A strong point, but you haven't won me over yet. Encouraging is better than requiring.

grammar.title: Debate language
grammar.ar: في المناظرة: قدّم موقفك، ادعمه بمثال، ثم ردّ على الحجّة المضادة بأدب.
examples: I'd like to make a case against the motion.
To back this up, let me give you an example.
My opponent claims it's too hard, but that isn't true.

words.ex: I missed out on the trip because I was ill.
We missed the flight by a few minutes.
If only I had checked the time!
If we had set off earlier, we'd have been fine.
We caught the train, but it was a close call.
The trip turned out to be the best of the summer.

dialogue.t: Weren't you supposed to be in Abha last weekend? What happened?
We missed the flight by a few minutes. There was a huge traffic jam on the way to the airport.
Oh no! Did you leave late?
A bit. If we had set off half an hour earlier, we would have caught the plane.
So you missed out on the whole trip?
No, we flew the next morning. If only my dad hadn't wanted one more coffee before leaving!
Ha! Well, at least it turned out fine in the end.
True. On the way back we nearly missed the plane again. That was a close call, so now we leave three hours early.

grammar.title: Third conditional
grammar.ar: نستخدم If + had + التصريف الثالث، ثم would have + التصريف الثالث للحديث عن ماضٍ لم يحدث.
examples: If we had left earlier, we would have caught the plane.
If I hadn't overslept, I wouldn't have missed the trip.
We might have won if we had practised more.

words.ex: Salem hit the post in the last minute.
The red card was the turning point.

words.ar: كان من الممكن أن تميل لأي طرف
words.ex: It was so close it could have gone either way.
Don't blame the loss on the referee.
In hindsight, we should have defended more.
Our keeper saved it, but it was a close call.

dialogue.t: I still can't believe it. If we had taken that first chance, we would have won easily.
I know. Honestly, it could have gone either way until the last ten minutes.
Exactly. If our striker hadn't hit the post, everything might have been different.
In hindsight, the red card was the turning point. We were playing with ten men after that.
Some fans are blaming the defeat on the referee, but I think it was a fair decision.
Me too. If our defender had stayed calm, he wouldn't have been sent off.
And their striker nearly scored a third in the last minute. That was a close call!
Well, there's always next season. We could have done worse!

grammar.title: Third conditional with might / could
grammar.ar: استخدم might have أو could have بدلاً من would have عندما لا تكون متأكداً من النتيجة.
examples: If he hadn't hit the post, we might have won.
We could have scored more if we had passed faster.
If the referee had seen it, he would have given a penalty.

words.ex: Who came up with the idea of the internet?
The printing press changed the course of history.
Without electricity, we couldn't use our phones.
Penicillin was discovered by accident in 1928.
We take clean water for granted.
His mistake turned out to be a great discovery.

dialogue.t: Let's start with penicillin. Fleming discovered it by accident when he left some lab dishes out before a holiday.
Lucky mistake! If he hadn't been so untidy, he wouldn't have noticed the mould.
And millions of people might have died from simple infections.
We really take medicine for granted, don't we?
What about Al-Jazari? He came up with amazing machines over 800 years ago.
Yes, his water clocks and robots. Some engineers think his ideas changed the course of history.
If nobody had built those early machines, modern engineers might not have developed robots so quickly.
So history turned out the way it did partly because of one curious inventor. Great project idea!

grammar.title: Third conditional in the passive
grammar.ar: عند الحديث عن الاختراعات نستخدم المبني للمجهول: If + had been + التصريف الثالث.
examples: If the plane hadn't been invented, people would have travelled by ship.
Without electricity, the internet would never have existed.
If penicillin hadn't been discovered, many more people would have died.

words.ex: I made a decision to join the swimming club.
I ended up loving a subject I used to hate.
All those hours of practice finally paid off.
If I had given up piano, I wouldn't play today.
If I had started earlier, I'd be fluent in French now.
In hindsight, joining the club was a great choice.

dialogue.t: Your English is amazing now, Mishari. How did you get so good?
When I was ten, I made a decision to watch cartoons only in English. It really paid off.
I wish I'd done that. If I had started earlier, I'd be fluent now.
It's not too late! You're only fifteen.
True. But I gave up drawing at twelve, and in hindsight that was a mistake.
Why? You were so talented.
If I hadn't given up, I would probably be studying design at the art academy now.
Then start again! You might end up loving it even more.

grammar.title: Mixed conditional (past → present)
grammar.ar: الشرط في الماضي (had + التصريف الثالث) والنتيجة في الحاضر (would + الفعل): If I had started earlier, I would be fluent now.
examples: If I had started earlier, I would be fluent now.
If I hadn't joined the team, I wouldn't know my best friend.
She would be a doctor today if she had studied medicine.

words.ex: Meeting the coach was a lucky break.
I happened to be there when the scout arrived.

words.w: the right place at the right time
words.ex: She was in the right place at the right time.
My brother is outgoing, so he makes friends easily.
He made a quick decision and it worked.
We ended up winning the competition.

dialogue.t: How did you get a part in that film? You've never acted before!
Pure luck. I happened to be at the café when the director was looking for teenagers.
So you were in the right place at the right time.
True. If I weren't so outgoing, I wouldn't have spoken to him at all.
I'm the opposite. I'm quite shy. If it had been me, I would have just watched.
And if my uncle didn't live in AlUla, I wouldn't have been there in the first place.
What a lucky break! So what happened next?
I ended up with two lines in the film. If I hadn't said hello, I wouldn't be a 'film star' now!

grammar.title: Mixed conditional (present → past)
grammar.ar: حالة دائمة في الحاضر (If + الماضي البسيط) تفسّر نتيجة في الماضي (would have + التصريف الثالث).
examples: If I weren't so outgoing, I wouldn't have spoken to him.
If my uncle didn't live there, I wouldn't have visited.
If she weren't so talented, she wouldn't have been chosen.

words.ex: Moving to Jeddah was a turning point for our family.
It all started when my father bought an old camera.
Engineers finally struck oil in 1938.
The new metro has transformed travel in Riyadh.
The team was on the verge of giving up.
One well changed the course of history.

dialogue.t: It all started when American geologists began drilling near Dammam in the 1930s.
And they didn't find anything at first, right?
No. They were on the verge of giving up after six dry wells.
So if they had stopped then, they would never have found the oil?
Exactly. They kept drilling and struck oil at Well No. 7 in 1938. It was a real turning point.
It transformed the whole country, didn't it?
Completely. If they hadn't kept going, the Kingdom would probably look very different today.
Amazing. One decision not to give up changed the course of history.

grammar.title: Third and mixed conditionals together
grammar.ar: في قصة نقطة التحوّل: استخدم الشرط الثالث لنتيجة في الماضي، والمختلط لنتيجة في الحاضر.
examples: If they had stopped drilling, they would never have found oil.
If they hadn't found oil, the country would be very different now.
If I hadn't moved schools, I wouldn't have met my best friend, and I'd be less confident today.

words.ex: Today I'd like to talk about falconry.
I've divided my talk into three parts.
Let me start by explaining how I got interested.
I got into calligraphy when I was eleven.
My grandfather has a passion for falcons.
A surprising fact is a great way to grab attention.

dialogue.t: Did you know that a single page of Arabic calligraphy can take days to finish? Today I'd like to talk about calligraphy.
Great opening! That fact really grabs attention.
Thanks. I've divided my talk into three parts: its history, the main styles, and why I love it.
Very clear. Then what?
Let me start by telling you how I got into it. My grandmother showed me her pens when I was nine.
Nice. A personal story makes the audience care.
